steps.premise: A performer's footwear can change where the trouser hem falls.
steps.action: Send each performer a brief list of what to bring or wear, including the show shoes when measuring trousers.
steps.consequence: The fitter sees the hem at the height it will sit in the show.
steps.quote: Send each performer a short list of what to wear or bring, since a trouser hem measured over slippers may sit differently over the show shoes.

steps.premise: Several changes or an elaborate costume can run over an ordinary appointment.
steps.action: Give performers with multiple changes extra time.
steps.consequence: The following fittings can start on schedule.
steps.quote: Allow a little extra time for people with several changes, so one elaborate costume doesn't quietly push the rest of the evening behind.

steps.premise: Standing on one leg can make changing awkward.
steps.action: Put a chair in the screened changing area.
steps.consequence: Performers can sit while changing.
steps.quote: Set up a screened changing area with a chair and hooks so nobody has to balance on one foot or leave their own clothes on the floor.

steps.premise: People need somewhere to put the clothes they take off.
steps.action: Fit hooks in the screened changing area.
steps.consequence: Performers can keep their own clothes off the floor.
steps.quote: Set up a screened changing area with a chair and hooks so nobody has to balance on one foot or leave their own clothes on the floor.

steps.premise: A performer may prefer to adjust the garment themselves.
steps.action: Get permission and wait for their response before touching them to adjust the clothing.
steps.consequence: They can choose to move the fabric themselves.
steps.quote: Ask before touching a performer to adjust a collar or sleeve, giving them time to say they'd prefer to move the fabric themselves.

steps.premise: Searching for a missing matching piece uses appointment time.
steps.action: Hang each complete outfit together, ordered by scene.
steps.consequence: The fitter can use the appointment to check the clothing.
steps.quote: Hang every part of an outfit together in scene order so a fitter can spend the appointment checking clothes instead of hunting for the matching waistcoat.

steps.premise: Someone arriving might walk in on a performer who is changing.
steps.action: Station a person immediately outside the fitting space to check arrivals in.
steps.consequence: People can arrive without interrupting a change.
steps.quote: Have someone check people in just outside the fitting area, which keeps arrivals from wandering into a change already in progress.

steps.premise: A travel delay can leave an appointment empty.
steps.action: Give performers one named person to notify if they are running late.
steps.consequence: The team hears in time to use the opening.
steps.quote: Let performers send word to one named contact if their journey is delayed, so the team can fill a gap while there's still time to use it.

steps.premise: A seam can bind during a movement the role requires.
steps.action: Have the performer try those movements while wearing the costume.
steps.consequence: The team can spot the restriction during the fitting.
steps.quote: Try the movements the role actually calls for, such as sitting on a low stool or raising both arms, to catch a tight seam while the performer is present.

steps.premise: The person doing the sewing later needs to identify the piece and which side to alter.
steps.action: Record the garment and the side from the wearer's point of view on every note.
steps.consequence: The sewer can carry out the change without someone demonstrating it.
steps.quote: Give each alteration note a garment name and the wearer's left or right side. The person sewing tomorrow should be able to pick it up without a demonstration.

steps.premise: Rubbing may take time to notice and be invisible in the mirror.
steps.action: After the performer has worn the outfit for a few minutes, ask where it rubs.
steps.consequence: Their account identifies discomfort that a visual check could miss.
steps.quote: Ask the performer where anything rubs after they've had the costume on for a few minutes, because discomfort doesn't always show in the mirror.

steps.premise: The performer needs a chance to judge the proposed change before cutting.
steps.action: Clip the change in place temporarily and let the wearer see it in the mirror.
steps.consequence: The wearer can give feedback while the fabric is still intact.
steps.quote: Use removable clips to hold a proposed change while the performer looks in the mirror, so they can comment before any fabric gets cut.

steps.premise: Finished garments could get swept into the alterations pile at cleanup.
steps.action: Put stage-ready garments on a dedicated rail.
steps.consequence: They stay separate when the room is cleared.
steps.quote: Reserve a rail for garments ready to go onstage, keeping them out of the alterations pile when the room is cleared at the end.

steps.premise: A fitter needs to watch the time while attending to the wearer.
steps.action: Put a legible clock where the fitter can see it.
steps.consequence: They can pace the session while keeping their attention on the performer.
steps.quote: Keep an easy-to-read clock within the fitter's sight so they can pace an appointment without repeatedly looking away from the performer.

steps.premise: A photo could help the sewer, but the performer may prefer to decline.
steps.action: If a picture would be useful, ask the performer's permission first.
steps.consequence: The performer can decide whether the photo is taken.
steps.quote: If a reference photo would help the sewer, ask permission and frame just the garment detail that needs work, leaving room for a performer to decline.

steps.premise: The sewer needs a record of a particular detail.
steps.action: For a permitted reference photo, frame just the part of the garment that needs work.
steps.consequence: The resulting image shows only the relevant detail.
steps.quote: If a reference photo would help the sewer, ask permission and frame just the garment detail that needs work, leaving room for a performer to decline.

steps.premise: A misunderstanding about a measurement is quick to fix while the performer is wearing the costume.
steps.action: Have the person taking notes read the alteration request back then.
steps.consequence: The team can correct the note on the spot.
steps.quote: Have the note taker read back the requested change while the costume is still on, when a misunderstood sleeve length takes seconds to put right.

steps.premise: Preparing an accessible changing space may take advance notice.
steps.action: At booking, invite the performer to share access needs privately.
steps.consequence: The team has time to arrange a suitable space before the fitting.
steps.quote: Invite people to mention access needs privately when booking, giving the team time to arrange a suitable changing space before they arrive.

steps.premise: Fastening a well-fitting costume might still take longer than a quick change allows.
steps.action: Allow a few minutes to try the fastest backstage change with the dresser.
steps.consequence: The team can discover whether the fastenings can be managed in time.
steps.quote: Set a few minutes aside for testing the fastest backstage change with the dresser, since a perfectly fitted jacket can still take too long to fasten.

steps.premise: The owner may require a borrowed piece to be returned without certain changes.
steps.action: Attach the owner's alteration restrictions to the borrowed garment on the rail.
steps.consequence: Volunteers can avoid making a prohibited change.
steps.quote: Mark borrowed pieces on the rail with the owner's alteration limits, saving a volunteer from shortening a hem that must be returned intact.

steps.premise: Refreshments near the costumes can spill on them.
steps.action: Put waiting volunteers' food and drinks on a separate table.
steps.consequence: A spill is less likely to soil a costume.
steps.quote: Keep drinks and snacks on a separate table for waiting volunteers so a long evening's coffee doesn't end up on a pale costume.

steps.premise: After the team goes home, a note alone may leave responsibility unclear.
steps.action: Before packing up, give each approved alteration to a specific sewer.
steps.consequence: Everyone knows who will carry out each change.
steps.quote: Assign each approved alteration to a particular sewer before packing up, making it clear who will act on a note once everyone goes home.

steps.premise: Performers' work shifts can make a fixed slot impractical.
steps.action: Reserve a short, separate window for drop-in fittings.
steps.consequence: Those performers can attend while booked guests keep their place.
steps.quote: Set aside a short drop-in window for performers whose shifts make a fixed appointment hard to keep, without making the booked guests wait behind them.

steps.premise: Dim room light can hide fastenings and seams on dark clothing.
steps.action: Put a lamp by the mirror that lights those details.
steps.consequence: The team is less likely to miss a needed change.
steps.quote: Use a lamp near the mirror that lets the team see fastenings and seams on dark fabric, cutting down on changes missed in a dim rehearsal room.

steps.premise: Some changes need checking again, and the wearer and garment are present now.
steps.action: Circle the changes requiring a refit and settle a return time with the wearer then.
steps.consequence: The team has a record of what to recheck and when the wearer will return.
steps.quote: Circle any change that needs another fitting and agree on a return time with the wearer, while their schedule and the garment are both to hand.

steps.premise: The amount of sewing may exceed the time available before a garment is needed.
steps.action: If that happens, write down the priorities the team agrees on.
steps.consequence: Sewers can tackle imminent rehearsal needs in time.
steps.quote: Write down the agreed priorities if there's more sewing than the team can finish, so a costume needed at tomorrow's rehearsal gets attention in time.
